doc.title: Joe Segal — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Race and neighborhoods in Chicago; Cabrini housing and his marriage
summary: He describes Chicago's racial geography, the jazz center at 63rd and Cottage, living in the mixed Cabrini project, and his Black wife and five children.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up under segregation: schools, neighborhoods, Jim Crow

blocks.x: So would you say that - of course we’re talking about, you know, Chicago being a benefit of the Great Migration there, so... what do you call it... Desegregation or tolerance or... there was more openness and understanding of base humanity, and not necessarily this whole notion of race divide. Is that something that was more common?
I don’t know about that, because most of the black population was on the south side or the west side.

The north was predominately white, and in fact the jazz center was at 63rd and Cottage, and there’d be fifteen, twenty clubs within a radius of five or six blocks. You could hear all kind of jazz there. I don’t know, I guess individuals moved up as their economics would permit them to. I got in a friend of mine from Roosevelt, worked with the CHA, the Chicago Housing Authority, and he got me into the Cabrini project.

The CHA, yes it was row houses, and it was fine and it was mixed. White and black. And my wife was black. I married her, and we had five kids, including my youngest, Wayne, who now actually is owner of the Jazz Showcase, and he’s the one who built this room in fact. Nothing bad happened there until they built the high-rises, and then the gangs came in. That’s when shit hit the fan.
